content: The treatment of multidrug-resistant and rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (TB), as well as extrapulmonary TB, post-TB care, and rehabilitation for TB-related functional impairments, should be provided in specialized facilities. These facilities should focus on adult and pediatric chest and TB care, nutrition, HIV, adolescent health, antenatal care (ANC), immunization, and dedicated screening events. Following screening, appropriate management or referral to TB preventive, treatment, and rehabilitative care services should be ensured. Symptom screening, chest X-rays, or molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests should be utilized either alone or in combination. In settings with a high burden of TB, bidirectional screening for COVID-19 and TB should be considered. If adolescents under 15 years of age are in close contact with someone with TB, systematic screening for TB disease should be conducted. This screening involves identifying individuals with symptoms such as cough, fever, or poor weight gain and may include chest radiography. Community health workers, outreach workers, and primary care providers should be engaged to scale up active contact tracing, provide family-integrated TB treatment and preventive therapy, and support adolescents receiving care. Healthcare professionals must recognize air pollution as a significant risk factor for their patients and understand the sources of environmental exposure in the communities they serve. This includes educating patients about the causes and consequences of indoor air pollution and promoting household mitigation measures. Efforts to reduce exposure to indoor air pollution should include switching from wood, dung, or charcoal to more efficient and less polluting fuels, placing stoves outside or in well-ventilated areas, ventilating cooking spaces with eaves and smoke hoods, and adopting behavioral changes such as keeping children away from smoking hearths, drying fuel wood before use, using lids on pots to shorten cooking time, and improving ventilation by opening windows and doors. To address diarrheal diseases, structural and environmental interventions should include implementing water safety plans and guidelines for drinking-water quality at the national level, sanitation safety plans for the safe use and disposal of wastewater and excreta, and policies promoting widespread adoption of proper hand-washing practices. Schools and healthcare facilities should be equipped with adequate water and sanitation infrastructure, as this can significantly reduce school absenteeism due to diarrheal diseases. Expanded hand-washing programs in schools, including the provision of soap and peer hygiene monitors, can further reduce absenteeism. Water treatment programs, such as the use of LifeStraw filters, ceramic water purifiers, and BioSand filters, should be scaled up to reduce diarrheal diseases by nearly 40%. Communities should be educated about water safety and improved sanitation measures, including safe storage of household water and access to basic sanitation facilities. Good hand-washing practices, such as washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet, should be maintained. Vaccination programs should be expanded in line with WHO recommendations to achieve high vaccination coverage. Strategies should focus on geographical units, mass gatherings, and improving infection prevention and control programs. Vaccination can also help combat antimicrobial resistance by reducing the need for antibiotics. Community awareness campaigns should address myths and vaccine hesitancy, particularly for diseases like meningitis. Integrated communication programs can increase awareness of the risks, symptoms, and consequences of meningitis and sepsis, as well as the recommended health-seeking responses. Meningitis can lead to severe long-term complications, including neurological issues such as hearing loss, visual impairment, seizures, and learning difficulties. Adolescents may also experience depressive symptoms and fatigue, which can impact educational attainment and quality of life. Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) such as cancer, migraines, skin diseases, and asthma are significant contributors to adolescent morbidity and mortality. Congenital anomalies and iron deficiency anemia also add to the disease burden. Many NCDs in adulthood originate from risk factors experienced during adolescence, such as tobacco use, which can lead to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or cancer later in life. Interventions targeting adolescents are crucial to protect their health in both the short and long term. For leukemia and other cancers in adolescents, WHO provides detailed guidance on planning, prevention, early detection, diagnosis, treatment, palliative care, and policy advocacy. In low-resource settings, where access to full treatment for acute lymphocytic leukemia is limited, recommendations include incorporating essential medications into national lists, improving diagnostic and treatment services, and developing strategies to enhance treatment adherence. Recent evidence supports the efficacy of motor and exercise interventions for adolescents with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, as well as digital interventions to improve health behaviors and reduce cancer-related symptoms. Asthma management involves addressing symptoms such as cough, wheezing, and difficulty breathing, which can vary daily and worsen with exposure to triggers like dust, fumes, smoke, and viral infections. Long-term management with inhaled medications, including corticosteroids, can improve daily symptoms and reduce asthma attacks. Effective management is essential to prevent school absences and reduce the need for emergency healthcare, which can impose financial burdens on families and health systems. Skin diseases in adolescents can lead to long-term disfigurement, disability, and stigma, contributing to psychological burdens such as anxiety and depression. WHO has developed a pictorial training guide for frontline health workers to improve the management of skin-related diseases, particularly those associated with neglected tropical diseases. Patient education has been shown to improve quality of life and reduce the severity of skin diseases, even in the long term. Detailed guidance on diagnosing and managing conditions like acne and eczema is available in the WHO IMAI District Clinician Manual. Cervical cancer, primarily caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), is the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide. HPV vaccination programs for girls aged 9–14 years are highly effective in preventing HPV infections, precancerous lesions, and invasive cancer. Some countries have also started vaccinating boys to prevent HPV-related diseases and cancers. Regular screening and treatment of precancerous lesions are essential, particularly in lowand middle-income countries where access to preventive measures is limited. WHO recommends promoting condom use, providing sex education, and encouraging male circumcision to reduce HPV transmission. Unaddressed sensory impairments, such as vision and hearing loss, in adolescents can often be prevented or treated. WHO recommends increasing access to spectacles or contact lenses, regular screening for refractive errors, and public health campaigns to reduce near-vision activities and encourage outdoor time to slow the progression of myopia. For hearing loss, awareness campaigns on healthy ear care and safe listening, adoption of WHO standards for safe listening devices, and regular school-based screening for hearing problems are recommended. Mental health conditions among adolescents are alarmingly prevalent, with up to 50% of all mental health conditions beginning before age 14. Suicide is a leading cause of death among older adolescents. Poor mental health is associated with high-risk behaviors, including self-harm, substance use, and risky sexual behaviors. The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated mental health challenges, increasing the risk of suicide and other mental health problems among young people.
